title: Your Best Catering Account Might Look Like Three Different Customers
summary: Your Best Catering Account Might Look Like Three Different Customers by PAR Technology . Catering . Click to learn more now.
body_markdown:
Here’s a month of catering activity at a typical restaurant:


## Jane orders


## $1,200


## of lunch for a team meeting.


## Two weeks later, John orders


## $850


## for a new-hire onboarding.


## Priya asks for a


## $2,500


## quote for an executive offsite.


## Jane comes back with a


## $1,400


## order.


In most order systems, that’s three customers, three tickets, and one open quote. Nothing about it stands out.


Except Jane, John, and Priya all work for Acme Corp.


Seen that way, Acme isn’t three customers. It’s one account with three buyers, $3,450 in completed business, and a $2,500 event still undecided. It may be one of your most active catering relationships, and there’s a real chance no one on your team sees it that way.


That gap is easy to live with when catering is small. As the program grows, it starts costing you business you’ve already earned.


### Same activity, two very different pictures


Order management answers the questions that keep today running: what was ordered, when it’s due, where it’s going. Account management answers the questions that decide what happens next: who you’re really doing business with, and whether that relationship is growing or slipping.


Put the Acme activity through both lenses and the difference is hard to miss.


The order view The account view


Customers Three unrelated individuals One organization with three buyers


Revenue Three separate tickets $3,450 from a single account


Priya’s quote A new lead, worked from scratch A $2,500 expansion opportunity with a proven customer


If Jane changes jobs One customer lost An account at risk, with two buyers still worth a call


Who on your team knows Whoever took each order Anyone who opens the account


In B2B catering, the person placing the order is rarely the whole customer. Jane may be the office manager, John may sit in HR, and Priya may plan executive meetings. Each buys independently, on behalf of the same company. Treat them as strangers to each other, and your catering business looks smaller and more scattered than it really is.


### What slips through when you only see orders


Missing the account rarely looks like a mistake in the moment. Every order still goes out on time. The cost shows up later, in business that quietly goes somewhere else.


## The warm quote gets treated like a cold lead.


Priya’s $2,500 request sits in the same pile as every other inquiry. No one connects it to an account that has already ordered three times and liked what it got, so no one follows up with the urgency it deserves.


## The quiet account goes unnoticed.


Jane stops ordering. Maybe she left Acme, maybe a competitor reached her first. Without an account view, there’s no signal that Acme went dark, and no prompt to call John or Priya before the relationship fades.


## What your team knows walks out the door.


Your catering manager remembers that Jane needs individually packaged meals and that John mentioned an event next month. Then that manager takes a vacation or takes a new job, and Acme’s next call starts from zero.


None of these are execution problems. They’re visibility problems, and they compound as catering grows


### Read the signals, then pick your moves


Account management doesn’t mean calling every customer who ever ordered a tray of sandwiches. A company that placed one small order six months ago may need nothing from you right now. The point is to spot the accounts where a little attention returns a lot.


Those accounts tend to send clear signals: more than one buyer, an open high-value quote, orders coming more often, or a busy account that suddenly goes silent. Each one calls for a different move.


**Example framework: Know where to focus**


Signal What it may mean Your move


Several buyers from one organization The relationship is spreading across teams Grow. Map who’s ordering and look for departments or events you haven’t served yet.


An open high-value quote Revenue is close but not committed Close. Follow up while the event date is still ahead of you.


Orders arriving more often The account is building a habit Protect. Keep execution flawless and get ahead of the next occasion.


An active account goes quiet A buyer moved on, or a competitor got in Win back. Check in, ask what changed, and reach the other buyers.


One small order, months ago Little engagement so far Monitor. Keep it visible without heavy effort.


*Your tiers will look different depending on your brand and your customers. What matters is the principle: different accounts earn different levels of attention.*


### Make what your team knows stick


Every signal in that table depends on one thing: the restaurant has to remember what it knows.


Right now, much of that memory lives in people. It’s in a catering manager’s inbox, a shared spreadsheet, a calendar note, or simply in someone’s head. That works until it doesn’t. A busy week, a sick day, or a resignation is all it takes for an account’s history to disappear.


The fix is to turn customer knowledge into restaurant knowledge. That means keeping each account’s buyers and contacts, order history, leads, quotes, activities, and next steps in one shared place, so anyone on the team can pick up the relationship where the last person left it.


This is where a CRM built for catering earns its keep. Jane’s order, John’s order, and Priya’s quote stop being three disconnected records and become one story about Acme Corp. And a story is something your team can act on.


### Deliver the order. Grow the account.


None of this replaces great order management. Catering still lives or dies on accurate orders that arrive on time. But delivering the business you’ve won and finding the business you haven’t are two different jobs, and they need different tools.


PAR Catering is built to do both:


-


**CRM and account management** connect individual buyers to the organizations they order for, so Acme shows up as Acme.


-


**Lead and quote management** keep potential business visible, and in context, before it becomes an order.


-


**Task and activity management** turn "I'll follow up next week" into a next step the whole team can see.


Your next big catering opportunity may not require a new customer at all. It could already be sitting inside an account with a second buyer, an open quote, or an order history that just went quiet.


So the question to ask isn’t only how many catering orders you have. It’s which accounts are behind them, and which one deserves a call this week.
